strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem: maintaining useful conversational memory over long interactions while reducing context length.

Nemori presents a coherent end-to-end architecture combining semantic boundary detection, narrative episodic memories, prediction-gap-based semantic memories, and unified retrieval. The presentation and diagrams make the high-level pipeline easy to understand.

Evaluation covers two established long-term-memory benchmarks, two LLM backbones, several contemporary memory baselines, component ablations, retrieval-depth sensitivity, and token/latency measurements.

The reported results are promising in specific areas. Nemori substantially improves temporal reasoning on LoCoMo and preference questions on LongMemEvalS, while using much less answer-time context than the full-context baseline.
The paper acknowledges some unfavorable results, including losses on fine-grained single-session questions and, for one backbone, overall LoCoMo performance below full context.
weaknesses: The experiments do not directly validate the central segmentation claim. There is no comparison or ablation replacing the proposed boundary detector with fixed-token chunks, interaction pairs, sessions, or another topic-segmentation method, nor any intrinsic boundary-quality evaluation. Consequently, the evidence does not establish that autonomous episodic segmentation causes the gains.

Evidence for the Predict-Calibrate mechanism is also insufficiently controlled. Nemori-s is only described as using direct semantic extraction; its prompt, output budget, number of LLM calls, and resulting memory size are not reported. Predict-Calibrate may receive more computation or produce more entries, so the performance difference does not by itself validate learning from prediction gaps.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a prompt-driven system. The manuscript omits the prompts for boundary detection, episode generation, prediction, distillation, answering, and judging; code or pseudocode detailed enough to reconstruct the pipeline; API/model snapshots; decoding parameters; run counts and seeds; index/update procedures; and complete baseline configurations. The LLM-generated confidence threshold is likewise not operationally specified.

The primary evaluation relies on a GPT-4o-mini judge without reporting its prompt, repeated-judgment protocol, agreement with humans, or robustness to another judge. Using the same model family within the evaluated systems and as judge creates an additional potential bias. The meaning of the displayed ± values is not explained.

Claims of significance and broad superiority are unsupported by statistical tests. LoCoMo contains only ten dialogues, making question-level comparisons potentially non-independent. Moreover, Nemori is not best across the board: it loses to other methods on several LoCoMo categories and trails full context overall with GPT-4.1-mini (0.794 versus 0.806).

The efficiency comparison counts answer-time context and latency but apparently excludes the substantial offline/online cost of repeated boundary detection, episode generation, prediction, calibration, embedding, and memory construction. Thus the claims of computational efficiency and scalability are not established through end-to-end token, latency, or monetary-cost measurements.

Baseline fairness is difficult to assess: proprietary Mem0 and Zep APIs may use different hidden models and settings, while Nemori uses the evaluated backbone throughout. RAG is represented by a single coarse 4096-token configuration. Stronger segmentation, summarization, and dual-memory controls are absent.

The method can rewrite dialogue into narratives and semantic facts, but the paper provides no factuality analysis, memory-quality evaluation, contradiction/update policy, or investigation of error propagation. LongMemEvalS knowledge-update results show that this is consequential, including a large degradation for GPT-4o-mini (78.2% to 61.5%).

The cognitive-science motivation is interesting but largely analogical. The implementation does not substantively derive from or test Event Segmentation Theory or the Free-energy Principle, and claims about genuine learning, self-evolution, and human-like memory go well beyond benchmark question answering.

Overall, the results are promising, but missing causal controls, incomplete evaluation rigor, and insufficient implementation details prevent establishing a sound and reproducible Findings contribution. A next-cycle revision could become competitive by releasing complete prompts/code, adding controlled segmentation and compute-matched distillation ablations, validating the judge, testing significance at the dialogue level, and reporting end-to-end costs and memory-factuality analyses.

strengths: The manuscript addresses a relevant NLP problem: retaining and retrieving information from long-running conversational interactions. The proposed pipeline—semantic boundary detection, narrative episodic memory, and distilled semantic memory—is coherent and easy to understand. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/a16715409203446d9160b7f69eb1d398/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Evaluation covers two established long-term-memory benchmarks, two backbone models, per-question-type results, an ablation, and retrieval-depth sensitivity. The LongMemEvalS results suggest that structured memory can substantially improve several categories while reducing inference-time context length.

The paper reports concrete resource-related measurements, including retrieved-token counts and latency, and acknowledges categories such as knowledge-update and single-session-assistant questions where compression can lose information.
The comparison between prediction-gap distillation and direct semantic extraction is potentially useful evidence, although it is insufficiently controlled in the present version.
weaknesses: The central mechanisms are not directly validated. There is no evaluation of boundary quality, no comparison against fixed-turn, session, or alternative topic segmentation under an otherwise identical pipeline, and no ablation of narrative generation. Consequently, the experiments cannot support the claimed importance of the Two-Step Alignment Principle.

The evidence for Predict-Calibrate is also confounded. Nemori-s and the full semantic-memory procedure may differ in prompts, generated content, and computation, but these factors are not controlled or analyzed. More seriously, Equation 4 retrieves prior semantic knowledge using an embedding of the new episode's title concatenated with its actual content, even though this retrieval is presented as preceding prediction of that content. This content-conditioned selection weakens the interpretation of the resulting discrepancy as a genuine prediction gap.

Reproducibility is inadequate for Findings. The paper supplies neither code nor complete prompts, and omits model/API snapshots, decoding settings, random seeds, run counts, judge prompts, database implementation details, baseline versions/configurations, construction costs, and enough procedural detail to recreate the reported memories. Mem0 and Zep additionally depend on opaque commercial APIs.

The evaluation protocol is insufficiently rigorous. The source of the reported plus/minus values is never explained, statistical significance is not tested, and the gpt-4o-mini judge is not validated against human judgments or an independent judge. Exact-match-style F1 and BLEU-1 do not repair possible judge bias, particularly for open-ended answers.

Several empirical claims overstate the tables. With gpt-4.1-mini, Nemori is worse than full context overall on LoCoMo (0.794 versus 0.806); with gpt-4o-mini, its 0.021 advantage lacks significance testing. It also loses notably on LoCoMo open-domain questions and on multiple LongMemEvalS categories. Thus the abstract and conclusion's broad claims of significantly surpassing prior systems and full context are not established.

The LongMemEvalS study compares only against full context, omitting all memory-system baselines. Results from two datasets with different protocols do not demonstrate that Nemori's advantage becomes more pronounced with context length, nor do they establish state-of-the-art performance on the longer benchmark.

The claimed efficiency advantage counts query-time tokens and latency but excludes the repeated LLM calls needed for boundary detection, episode generation, prediction, calibration, and memory construction. Without end-to-end token usage, monetary cost, storage, and indexing latency, the efficiency comparison is misleading. Calling full context a theoretical upper bound is likewise incorrect because Nemori performs additional offline computation that can derive facts absent from the raw answer-time representation.

The near-zero 'w/o Nemori' ablation appears to provide the answering model with essentially no usable conversation information, making it a trivial lower bound rather than evidence for the framework. The paper also provides only one favorable anecdote and no systematic error, hallucination, contradiction, or information-loss analysis.

The cognitive-science framing is largely metaphorical: the implementation consists primarily of LLM prompting and vector retrieval, with no formal derivation from or empirical test of Event Segmentation Theory, the Free-energy Principle, or Complementary Learning Systems. The terms 'genuine learning,' 'self-evolution,' and 'human-like learning' are therefore unsupported.

Overall, the idea is plausible and the preliminary benchmark results are promising, but the missing controlled ablations, incomplete comparisons, unclear evaluation statistics, and poor reproducibility prevent a sound Findings recommendation. A next-cycle resubmission could be viable after a substantially more controlled and transparent empirical study.

strengths: Nemori addresses an important NLP problem with a coherent architecture: semantic episode segmentation, narrative episodic memory, and prediction-gap-based semantic memory. The predict-calibrate mechanism is intuitive and potentially useful beyond this particular system.

The empirical results are promising across two established long-term conversational-memory benchmarks and two LLM backbones. Nemori substantially reduces answer-time context and improves average LongMemEvalS accuracy over full-context inference.
The component study provides useful evidence that episodic and semantic memories are complementary and that predict-calibrate semantic memories outperform the paper's direct-extraction variant.

The paper is clearly organized and motivates the design through concrete examples. It also reports category-level results, retrieval sensitivity, latency, and context-token consumption rather than only aggregate accuracy.
weaknesses: The evidence does not isolate the claimed innovation in episode formation. There is no intrinsic boundary-quality evaluation and no controlled comparison against fixed-size, turn-pair, session, or existing topic-segmentation alternatives. Thus the central claim that the Two-Step Alignment Principle solves the granularity problem remains largely unverified.

The predict-calibrate comparison is insufficiently controlled: Nemori-s may differ in prompts, inference budget, number or length of stored facts, and access to context. Without budget-matched extraction or summarization baselines and qualitative error analysis, the gain cannot confidently be attributed to learning from prediction gaps.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a prompt-driven system. The manuscript omits the prompts for boundary detection, episode generation, prediction, distillation, answering, and judging; it also lacks implementation details, code or artifact information, API/model versions, decoding settings, database configuration, and an explanation of the reported uncertainty estimates.

The evaluation relies heavily on a single unvalidated GPT-4o-mini judge, including evaluation of GPT-4o-mini-generated answers. Judge prompts, repeated-run protocol, human agreement, and statistical significance tests are absent. LoCoMo contains only ten dialogues, making dialogue-level uncertainty particularly important.

Some conclusions overstate the tables. Nemori does not outperform full context overall with GPT-4.1-mini on LoCoMo and loses on several question categories; it also substantially hurts GPT-4o-mini knowledge-update accuracy on LongMemEvalS. Claims of consistent or significant superiority are therefore unsupported as written.

The efficiency comparison counts answer-time context and latency but apparently omits the multiple LLM calls required to construct and continually update Nemori's memories. End-to-end token, monetary, latency, and storage costs are needed for the computational-efficiency claim. LongMemEvalS additionally compares only against full context, not the memory-system baselines.

The cognitive-science framing is mostly analogical: no experiment shows that the free-energy or event-segmentation interpretation explains the gains better than a simpler engineering account. Claims about genuine learning, human-like evolution, and a principled solution should consequently be moderated. Overall, the idea and results are encouraging, but missing controls and reproducibility details prevent a clear Findings recommendation in the current form.

strengths: The paper identifies a relevant problem in long-term LLM-agent memory and presents a coherent modular framework combining episode construction, narrative representations, semantic distillation, consolidation, and retrieval.

The empirical scope is relatively broad: two benchmarks, two backbone models, multiple memory baselines, construction and inference costs, component ablations, retrieval analyses, longer-context evaluation, and integrations with A-MEM and MemoryOS.

Results on LoCoMo are strong, particularly for temporal reasoning, while the LongMemEvalS results suggest that selective memory can outperform full-context inference with substantially fewer input tokens.

The episode-level processing strategy is practically appealing and is supported by markedly lower construction cost than the reported baselines. The third-party experiments also provide useful evidence that the distilled representation can reduce storage.

The paper is generally clear, and the appendix supplies algorithms, detailed category-level results, and the complete prompt templates, making the proposed pipeline substantially easier to understand and reimplement.
weaknesses: The central causal claim—that prediction-error distillation is responsible for the gains—is not adequately isolated. The main comparison is against a direct-distillation ablation whose prompt differs substantially in instructions, structure, and processing. A controlled ablation should remove only the anticipatory schema while holding the extraction prompt, inputs, calls, and token budget constant.

The claimed replacement of designer heuristics by a data-driven utility criterion is overstated. The system relies heavily on handcrafted rules and prompts specifying topic boundaries, persistence, factuality, future usefulness, merge behavior, and preferred memory categories. Moreover, the anticipatory schema is conditioned on an episode cue produced from the actual episode, potentially leaking its novel content into the prediction and making the resulting error sensitive to cue construction.

Temporal gains are seriously confounded by benchmark-targeted prompt engineering. Narrative generation explicitly converts relative dates to absolute dates, permits a 'reasonable estimate' when time is missing, and response generation again instructs date conversion. The temporal case study therefore does not establish that prediction error, rather than explicit preprocessing and temporal normalization, caused the improvement; the fallback also creates a hallucination risk that is not measured.

The evidence lacks uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, or significance tests. This is especially important because LoCoMo contains only ten dialogues and several reported differences are small. No analysis measures the stability of LLM-based partitioning, prediction, consolidation, or judging under stochastic generation.

The LongMemEvalS scalability evidence compares only against Full Context rather than the memory-system baselines used on LoCoMo. Some category results are highly uneven—for example, substantial degradation on knowledge-update questions with gpt-4o-mini—and the very large preference gains are not investigated. Per-category sample sizes and error analysis are also absent.

Baseline comparability and reproducibility are insufficiently documented. Some construction-cost numbers are imported from another study, Mem0 and Zep use unspecified commercial API versions, decoding settings and random seeds are omitted, and latency measurements lack hardware and measurement protocols. The manuscript says that code is available but displays no actual repository URL.

The third-party integration results are presented too favorably: temporal performance drops by roughly 13–38% after replacing raw input with distilled knowledge. Reporting a separate 'Core' score that excludes temporal reasoning obscures this important loss, even if aggregate accuracy remains close.

Overall, the work is promising and may become suitable for Findings, but the present evidence does not yet substantiate its main mechanistic and 'non-heuristic' claims. Controlled distillation ablations, uncertainty reporting, stronger long-context baselines, and complete reproducibility details are needed for a clear positive recommendation.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent, practically relevant memory pipeline combining episode segmentation, narrative representation, prediction-conditioned distillation, and consolidation. The distinction among distillation, management, and retrieval is conceptually useful.

Evaluation covers two long-conversation benchmarks, two backbone models, several competitive memory systems, efficiency, retrieval sensitivity, component ablations, and integration with two external systems.
The reported task results are often strong, particularly for temporal reasoning, and the large context reduction on LongMemEvalS is promising.

Algorithms, hyperparameters, and full prompts are included, substantially aiding inspectability and potential reproduction. The manuscript is also generally clear and well organized. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/599309dac6384446922113ac5f0ae3e7/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not adequately isolated. The comparison between prediction-error distillation and NEMORI-s changes the complete distillation prompt and information-processing procedure, rather than varying only the prediction-error mechanism. Thus the large gain cannot confidently be attributed to prediction error.

The claimed replacement of designer heuristics with a data-driven criterion is overstated. The system embeds extensive hand-designed judgments in its prompts and hyperparameters, including topic-shift rules, a 30-minute boundary, episode-length guidance, persistent-fact criteria, excluded information types, similarity thresholds, and retrieval counts.

The paper equates unpredictability with future utility without directly testing that relationship. Retrospective QA accuracy does not establish that unpredictable observations are more useful later, and no controlled analysis measures retention precision/recall, utility calibration, or failures involving important but predictable facts.

NEMORI retains raw episodes and generated narratives in addition to semantic memories. Consequently, the native-system results do not demonstrate that prediction-error distillation itself achieves selective retention or overall storage reduction; the storage experiment instead substitutes distilled knowledge into third-party systems under a materially different input condition.

Statistical reliability is insufficient. LoCoMo contains only ten dialogues, yet no repeated runs, confidence intervals, significance tests, or analysis of stochastic LLM decisions is reported. Several highlighted advantages over Full Context are only 0.2–1.0 points and cannot support strong superiority claims without uncertainty estimates.

Baseline fairness and reproducibility remain unclear. Commercial APIs and local implementations are mixed; exact API snapshots, decoding parameters, baseline configurations, tuning procedures, and run-level outputs are not specified. Construction-cost figures for baselines are imported from another study, limiting comparability.

The third-party integration evidence is presented too favorably. Average accuracy sometimes declines, while temporal-reasoning accuracy collapses by roughly 13–38%. Introducing a post-hoc 'Core' score that excludes this category obscures an important loss rather than demonstrating generally maintained performance.

The unified answer prompt requires responses shorter than 5–6 words even for LongMemEval preference tasks, which ordinarily assess substantive personalized responses. The paper does not justify this adaptation or show that Full Context and all systems receive equivalently suitable prompting.

LLM-as-judge evaluation uses a model from the same family as the evaluated generators, with no human validation or alternative judge. F1 and BLEU partly mitigate this on LoCoMo, but LongMemEvalS conclusions depend entirely on the judge.

Overall, the approach and empirical signals are promising, but important controlled experiments, uncertainty analysis, and narrower claims are required before the contribution meets the soundness threshold for Findings. These revisions appear feasible for a subsequent review cycle.

strengths: NEMORI offers a coherent and practically relevant decomposition of agent memory into episodic integration, prediction-error-based semantic distillation, and management. Treating predictability as a signal for redundancy is an interesting, intuitive contribution to long-context conversational memory.

The empirical results are consistently strong. NEMORI outperforms the tested memory systems on LoCoMo with two backbone models, remains competitive with or slightly exceeds full-context inference, and shows larger gains on the substantially longer LongMemEvalS benchmark while using 95–96% less context.

The evaluation is unusually broad for a systems paper: it covers answer quality, construction cost, inference latency, retrieval and window sensitivity, component ablations, two model backbones, and integration with A-MEM and MemoryOS. The third-party experiments support the claim that the distillation layer can reduce storage without materially reducing average downstream performance.
The paper is clearly organized, provides formal descriptions and full prompt templates, and separates construction from retrieval. These details substantially aid understanding and reproducibility.

The episode-centric implementation yields meaningful practical efficiency gains: fewer construction calls and tokens than the reported baselines, and much lower inference context and latency than full-context prompting.
weaknesses: The central causal claim about prediction error is not cleanly isolated. The principal comparison, NEMORI-s versus the semantic-only prediction-error variant, changes the prompting procedure and content-selection instructions in addition to introducing an anticipatory schema. Controls using a null, shuffled, irrelevant, or oracle schema—and a direct-distillation prompt matched in wording and budget—are needed to establish that prediction error itself causes the gains.

The framing overstates the departure from designer heuristics. The prompts explicitly encode judgments such as retaining persistent factual information, ignoring temporary states and emotions, preferring particular knowledge categories, splitting on specified topic and time rules, and using hand-selected thresholds and retrieval counts. The method is adaptive in an important sense, but it does not assess utility solely from intrinsic data properties as repeatedly claimed.

Uncertainty is not reported. LoCoMo contains only ten dialogues, LLM operations are stochastic, and many headline differences are small, yet there are no repeated runs, confidence intervals, significance tests, or judge-agreement checks. A single gpt-4o-mini judge is also used without validation against human judgments or an independent judge model.

The strongest scalability experiment compares only against Full Context on LongMemEvalS, rather than against the competitive memory baselines used on LoCoMo. It therefore establishes an advantage over long-context prompting but not state-of-the-art memory-system performance at 105K-token scale. Performance also drops substantially on some important categories, notably gpt-4o-mini knowledge updates and single-session assistant questions, which deserves deeper analysis.

Some efficiency comparisons are not fully controlled: construction costs for baselines are imported from another study, commercial APIs are used for some baselines, and latency is reported without variance, hardware/API conditions, or repeated measurements. Exact model snapshots, decoding settings, random seeds, failure handling, and baseline configurations are also insufficiently specified for reliable numerical reproduction.

The management-agnostic claim is only partially demonstrated. Integration remains system-specific, as the authors acknowledge, and replacing raw input with distilled knowledge causes large temporal-reasoning losses for both third-party systems even when the aggregate or non-temporal score is maintained.

Overall, the paper appears sound and promising, but the confounded central ablation, limited uncertainty analysis, and incomplete long-context baseline comparison prevent a confident main-conference recommendation. It is stronger than a routine Findings paper and is close to conference acceptance if these evidential gaps are addressed.
